This is the state called fanāʾ, or self-effacement, which brings joy to those who know God. It does not mean that two things become one. — س ره

Even so, the numbers that divide into a given number are close, natural features that arise from that number itself. In this sense, they are like essential features. Many questions in arithmetic and some less familiar sciences depend on them. — س ره
That is, number is made only from unity, and number comes about through repeating unity. This supports the author’s point. — س ره

Unity applies to itself, as existence applies to existence and knowledge to knowledge. It also applies to multiplicity, because every many has unity in some respect. Here “belonging to a subject” means being connected to, or attributed to, something, even as an idea. Unity is not something added only after its subject exists. — س ره

At first, the author’s wording seems to include likeness, while otherness in individual identity is called “other.” To understand “difference in a feature,” use the logical sense of a descriptive feature: it may be the subject itself, part of it, or something outside it. In another classification, things that share an essential feature are alike; if they do not share one, then they are either contraries that cannot coexist or different things that can. Here “contrary” means a difference in an essential feature. — س ره
The words “same” and “other” are used in different ways in different technical systems. In one, “other” means different in individual identity; in another, it means likeness. — س ره

The author may mean that some differences between kinds make coexistence impossible, not that this is always so. This is a claim about particular cases, not a universal rule. Many kinds under one broad category can coexist, such as sweetness and yellowness in honey. Some philosophers also count bodily matter and form as two kinds of substance. — ط مد

“Subject” means anything that can serve as a bearer, even one assumed only in thought. This includes a statement considered as the subject of affirmation and denial. The time condition applies only to things that exist in time; timeless cases do not need it. A shared subject is essential to opposition: each side excludes the other from the same bearer. — ط مد

The phrase “in the same respect” is needed for paired relations such as father and son. It does not exclude the case of Zayd, who can be both a father and a son, because he is a father in relation to one person and a son in relation to another. The two general relations themselves are opposites.
The objections apply to the second way of dividing opposition, not the first. In the first division, one side is already defined as the absence of the other. — س ره

The two meanings do not even apply to exactly the same things. “Not blind” can be said of something that does not exist, because denial does not require a subject. Sight, however, requires an existing subject. — س ره
If the first account is correct, then opposition outside affirmation and denial is indirect rather than direct. — ط مده

The objection assumes that “removal,” in the phrase “the opposite of each thing is its removal,” means denial in the usual sense. The author points out that this would make only one side of a contradiction the true opposite. He then proposes using “removal” in a broader sense that can describe either side. — ط مده
Affirmation does not deny its opposite; it is what the denial rejects. — ه ره
The opposite of “not human” is not simply “human”; it is the denial of “not human,” which implies “human.” — ه ره

The better account mentioned here is the one the author develops later in the section on God and creation: “removal” includes both the idea of removing something and the real instance of its being removed. — ن ره

This is like the Arabic word for “praise” in “Praise belongs to God”: it can mean the act of praising or the state of being praised. The general word for “removal” can likewise mean either removing or being removed. — س ره
In other words, we can say either “its opposite is what removes it” or “its opposite is what is removed.” — ه ره
The contrast is between Zayd’s being white and his not being white. These are not complete statements. — س ره

If we add “not” to an idea simply as an idea, we get another idea, separate from the first just as any two ideas are. But if “not” means that something does not exist, the idea concerns whether a real thing exists, and the contrast becomes one between statements. This shows that contradiction in the full sense is between statements. The apparent contradiction between single terms such as “human” and “not human” depends on the positive and negative statements in which they appear. At its root is the rule that either the affirmation or the denial is true, but never both or neither. — ط مده
The author says this because the opposition between affirmation and denial applies both to statements and to single terms. — س ره
The two statements cannot both be true of the same case. The author later explains that they cannot both be true, but may both be false when there is no subject. — س ره

I say that al-Tusi, as explained in Al-Shawāriq, means that this opposition does not concern things existing outside the mind. In a contradiction, affirmation and denial concern relations that exist only in the mind, when we think a statement, or in speech, when we utter it. Opposition is itself a relation: a relation between relations. Indeed, the negative relation is the denial of the relation. It is surprising that the author himself acknowledges this a few lines later when he says that their opposition exists only in the mind, or figuratively in speech. That was all al-Tusi intended. Perhaps the author took him to be explaining what produces the opposition, or which side is opposed directly and which indirectly. But al-Tusi was identifying what the opposition applies to. — س ره

Calling universal affirmative and negative statements “contraries” stretches the usual meaning of the word. The author’s own example shows that this is only a label, not a strict fit with the definition. — ط مد

“Relation” here means an explanatory connection, not a feature that describes one thing in terms of another. An essence and a necessary result may be connected, yet neither exists at the same level as the other. The same applies to paired relations. — س ره

The passage may seem to repeat itself, but it makes two different points. First, a subject cannot be without either affirmation or denial in reality. Second, at a particular level of reality, it may be neither present nor absent. The author also adds that the statements cannot both be true. — س ره

Paired relations such as fatherhood and sonhood are opposites because each is understood by reference to the other. Neither can be understood alone. Their opposition is part of what they are. Some of the author’s other remarks may suggest that relations such as knower and known can coexist, and that they fail to do so only for an outside reason, as with cause and effect. The commentator rejects that view. — ط مد

Do not confuse a concept with what it describes. The idea of “relation” is not itself a relation, but the things it describes may be related. In the same way, the idea of “opposition” is an idea about relations, while its examples may include other kinds of relation. — ن ره

The author offers three answers. The first distinguishes a feature from the things that bear it. The second distinguishes relation in general from the narrower kind of relation that is opposition. The third distinguishes defining an idea from applying it to actual examples. In that sense, the concept of opposition is opposition by definition, while an actual case of opposition may also be a paired relation. A mental concept can belong to one group and serve as an example of another when considered in different ways. — س ره

The author repeatedly says that the definition of contraries, and some of the rules connected with it, rest on convention. These include the claims that one thing has only one contrary, that contraries must belong to the same nearest general kind, and that substances cannot be contrary to one another. This suggests that he regards only the conditions produced by the division of opposites as essential to the definition. On that account, contraries are two existing, positive things that are not relative to one another and cannot be present in the same subject in the same respect. Anything added to this would rest on convention.

But it would be very strange to build philosophical conclusions on convention alone. If we add conditions to a definition that follows from a division, we create further possible kinds of opposition. We must either recognize and name these kinds or prove that they cannot exist.

The usual definition says that contraries are two positive things, neither defined in relation to the other, that take turns in one subject, belong to the same nearest general kind, and differ as far as possible. Here is how its conditions can be understood.

The first conditions follow from the earlier division of opposites. Either one opposite is the absence of the other, or both are positive. If both are positive, they are either understood through their relation to each other or they are not. The second pair are contraries: two positive things that are not relative terms.

Why must they have a subject? To call two things opposed, and different from each other in their very nature, we must consider a third thing with which either one can be united. The presence of one then excludes the other from that same third thing. Otherwise, the idea of opposition does no work. Since both contraries are positive, the third thing must be something in which a positive feature can exist. Here subject is used broadly. It may mean the matter that receives a substantial form or the subject that bears an accidental property.

Yet if we also require the greatest possible difference, substantial forms will not count as contraries. We are left with subjects that bear accidental properties. This is one reason for saying that contraries must be accidents, that they come in pairs, and that the two members take turns in a single subject.

Why, then, must both belong to one general kind? A substantial form is united in existence with its matter. Together they make one definite thing. If substantial forms could be contraries, that union itself would be enough for each to exclude the other from the matter with which it becomes one.

An accidental property is different. Its subject can exist without it. The subject and the property do not become a single reality in that same way. Simply saying that the two properties belong to one subject does not explain why one must exclude the other: one accident does not become identical with another merely because they share a subject.

We therefore need something else with which either contrary can be united so completely that it makes a single kind of thing. In that unity, each excludes the other, because allowing both would amount to making something exclude itself. What meets this description is a general kind, or broader kind, which includes its species. The two contraries must therefore come under one broader kind.

More precisely, it must be their nearest broader kind. A species is made definite by the distinguishing feature that divides and completes that nearest broader kind. A more distant broader kind does not have the same direct relation to the distinguishing feature. This was explained earlier in the discussion of essence. It follows that genuine contrariety occurs within a kind of accidental property divided into two species, with no third species between them.

Finally, why must the difference be the greatest possible? Philosophers first recognized opposition in such pairs as black and white. They then found intermediate colors, including yellow and red. These could be called white in comparison with black, or black in comparison with white. They were therefore treated as combinations lying between the two extremes, leaving the extreme ends as the real contraries.

On this account, the greatest possible difference means that the opposition is not a matter of comparison or changing points of view. The two sides differ in themselves. This last condition makes explicit what their opposition already means. — Ṭ. M.

The definition would be clearer if it said that contraries are positive things whose meanings do not depend on each other, that take turns in one subject, and so on. Paired relations can also take turns in one subject, but they are not contraries. — س ره
If good and evil were contraries, their opposition would be a paired relation. But they are not contraries: suitability and conflict are relations. — س ره
A better account is that virtue and vice are evaluative labels: they describe what should or should not be done. Vice also means a lack, as its definition makes clear. — ط مده
This assumes that there is no middle state between health and sickness. Some physicians say there are intermediate conditions, such as the state of a child, a young person, or an old person. — س ره
The author is returning to his earlier definition, which requires a shared subject, not merely a place where things exist. — س ره

The fact that kinds under a broad general kind do not oppose one another does not prove that sharing a nearest general kind causes opposition. It is possible that a shared kind plays no part at all. The author would need to show that contraries must share some kind. Also, the list of ten highest categories comes from observing examples; it is not a conclusion proved by reason alone. — ط مده

The earlier problem may have been about how a general kind and its defining features fit together. The defining features divide the general kind into its specific kinds; this does not mean that several separate causes act on one result. That is a different issue from whether two features can take turns in the same subject. The first reading is more precise. — س ره
Contrariety is a feature of things as they exist outside the mind. This does not rule out opposition between ideas in the mind, where the mind considers them in different ways.
The phrase “whether or not” refers to the positive feature: the subject may have the potential for it in itself, at a certain time, or as a member of a kind or broader group. — س ره

“Blindness” includes cases such as a scorpion’s or a person born unable to see. Hair loss from disease occurs after the subject had hair; hairlessness from birth occurs before that. Darkness is mentioned because some treat it as a positive contrary of light. — س ره

It is strange that he reverses the two established uses of “having and lacking.” Metaphysicians use the broader meaning and logicians the narrower one, as anyone who reads the Categories section of The Healing can see. In this book, the relevant lack is the loss of a capacity at the time when the subject should be able to act—for example, blindness after the power of sight has been lost. Having the capacity can give way to lacking it; once this particular capacity has been lost, the lack itself cannot simply become the capacity. By “this book,” the author of the quoted discussion means the Categories, the ancient title for the section on the ten categories of things in logic. Other sections were also given Greek titles, such as Isagoge for the five universals and Bārminās for propositions, as noted in the author’s commentary on The Healing and elsewhere. — س ره

This definition is only one part of the division. It focuses on whether the things can exist together in one subject. The different definitions add other conditions to separate contrary qualities from paired relations and from having and lacking. These conditions include being positive features, differing as much as possible, and having a subject that can move from one side to the other. — س ره

This supports the point that the terms are used in the reverse way described above. To include a tree’s lack of sight under contrariety, we need the broader, familiar meaning, which does not require both sides to be positive. A tree cannot see as an individual, as a kind, or through a nearby general kind; only a very broad underlying kind such as matter could be called capable of sight. The tree is not a problem for affirmation and denial, which also cover it. — س ره
Since the broader, familiar meaning does not require both sides to be positive, it can include these examples. They can also be included under the broader meaning of having and lacking. — س ره
As noted earlier, the familiar definition of contrariety is simply that the two sides cannot exist together in one subject. — س ره
On closer inspection, odd and even belong to affirmation and denial. The name “the One” used for God also points to this use of “one.” — س ره

In the earlier philosophers’ account, every shade of black is black in itself; it does not become white when compared with a darker shade. The claim that a middle shade is black relative to a lower shade and white relative to a higher one does not fit that account. — ن ره

The true unity found in existence does not oppose the different levels of multiplicity, which vary in how complete they are. This is unity within multiplicity and multiplicity within unity. As we have seen, multiplicity is nothing but unity repeated. The author’s difficulty is that he assumes one and many are opposed, then tries to decide which kind of opposition applies without first showing that they are opposed at all. What is clear is only that their meanings differ. — س ره

This follows from the usual rule about general ideas: each thing’s nature, considered in itself, is simply what it is. But in Mulla Sadra’s account, the particular existence of a possible thing is what is truly caused and brought into being; it is not the same as this general concept. — س ره
As they say, paired relations do not cause one another. Unity, by contrast, is a cause and comes first in its own right, while multiplicity is its effect and comes after it. — س ره

One could defend the author’s point by saying that the difference between the two unities comes from the different things in which they appear. Unity itself does not differ, and the size of the thing does not change the unity it receives. So the unity that contributes to a new multiplicity does so in the same way as unity contributes to multiplicity generally, once we set aside its link to a particular thing. Like cases should be treated alike, whether the result is allowed or not. Also, if the author’s opponent appealed to the mutual relation between measuring and being measured, this reply would not apply. — س ره
That is, the two opposing things must take turns in the same individual thing. — س ره
That is, two opposing things do not have to take turns in one individual thing. — س ره

Movement in a human being and rest in an inanimate thing illustrate opposition across a very broad shared kind. By contrast, the movement and rest of this same stone plainly take turns in one individual thing. Likewise, good and bad can refer, for example, to the goodness ascribed to God and to basic matter. — س ره
Defining features and necessary qualities oppose their negations in what we say about them, not in the way they exist, as the author explained earlier. — س ره
This refers to the appeal to desire in the argument. — س ره

This suggests that the four familiar kinds of opposition are not a fixed list proved by reason alone; the usual definition of contraries rests on accepted usage. What we can say for certain is that both one and many exist, and that they conflict in some way. Existence itself divides directly into one and many. These two ideas come from existence itself and are not outside it; otherwise, they would be false, since existence is what is fundamental. Unity and multiplicity are different features of existence, yet both belong to it. As explained earlier, unity goes with existence and applies to both one and many. Existence is shared by them and also differs in each. This is how one reality can have stronger and weaker levels. Many is the weaker level because the unity that goes with existence is weaker in it. This resembles other divisions: what exists outside the mind and what exists only in the mind; what is actual and what is only possible; what stays fixed and what changes. Different levels of one reality do not oppose one another in the strict sense, because their differences depend on what they share. So one and many, simply as one and many, are not opposites. The fact that one can appear when many disappears, and vice versa, shows only that they occupy different levels of one reality. — ط مده

Someone may object: a complete cause must include the absence of anything that blocks the effect. But absence is nothing; how can it help bring something into existence? Also, if a complete cause contains all the incomplete causes, it is not one thing but a collection made only in thought. The reply is that a complete cause can be simple, as the First Cause is for its first effect, or made up of several things, as causes in nature are. An agent that brings something into existence must itself exist. If “the complete cause exists” means that the agent exists along with all the conditions it needs to act, there is no problem. The effect may depend on something negative, such as the absence of a barrier, but that absence does not bring existence about; the agent does. Or the phrase may mean that each part of the cause is present or absent in the way needed: the agent, matter, form, and a condition contribute by being present; a barrier contributes by being absent; and a preparatory cause may contribute through either its presence or its absence. The author of The Mawāqif says that the absence of a barrier reveals a positive condition. For example, an open doorway reveals a space through which one can pass, and the absence of a support reveals a space where a roof can fall. We may know a positive condition only by noticing that something negative is absent, which can make it seem that the absence itself causes the effect. The same objection and reply apply to the next chapter’s claim that a cause must exist when its effect exists, and that an effect must exist when its complete cause exists. — س ره

The author avoids defining a complete cause as “everything a thing needs,” because that would make it sound as if a complete cause must be made up of parts. The First Cause of its first effect, for example, may be simple. “In the first sense” may qualify “complete cause,” or it may mean that this is an added meaning beyond the first definition: the first definition also applies to the last part of a complete cause, which can be called a cause in a narrower sense. So a complete cause is what brings an effect into existence, with no further cause beyond it. — س ره

Conditions and the removal of obstacles are also incomplete causes. They are often not listed separately, because they may be counted as part of the agent, understood as the complete cause that acts independently. Sometimes they are counted as part of matter, since a thing cannot receive a form until the right conditions are present and obstacles are removed. In his commentary on Al-Mulakhkhas, al-Jurjānī counts tools as part of the agent and the other factors as part of matter. The same applies to the second division: conditions and the removal of obstacles are causes that are not parts of the thing. The thing that receives an accidental feature is counted with matter because it is much like matter. If we consider a general kind and its distinguishing feature separately from the whole, the kind plays the role of matter and the feature the role of form. — س ره

Al-Jurjānī gives a more detailed division. An incomplete cause is something on which a thing depends in order to exist. It is either part of that thing or outside it. If it is outside, it is either what receives the effect—the underlying thing that bears an accidental feature, or the matter that receives a substantial form—or it is not a receiver. If it is not a receiver, it is either the agent, the purpose, or neither. In the last case it may be something positive, such as a condition, or something negative, such as the absence of an obstacle. A part is either a part in thought, such as a general kind or its distinguishing feature, or a physical part, such as matter or form. The phrase “it may be positive or negative” divides these cases without leaving any out; it also includes the preparatory cause. — س ره
That is, the same is true of the other one, form or matter. — س ره
The purpose, as understood in the mind, explains why the agent acts as an agent. Just as something’s being a purpose is not itself caused, an agent’s being an agent is not itself caused. — س ره

“Human form” here means the form that makes a human being the kind of thing it is, not the body’s shape. The form in the father brings about the same kind of form in the child. The ultimate agent is God, or, by God’s power, one of the beings close to Him. The passage does not mean the father’s physical shape. For Avicenna, the natural cause is the shaping power; for the Illuminationists, it is the intelligence that governs the species. It is not the father’s bodily form. — س ره

This objection applies to the view that the world began after a period of nonexistence, as the Ashʿarites held. They imagined that the world was preceded by empty stretches of time. In their view, freedom and necessity conflict, so they rejected the rule that a thing cannot bring about an effect until it becomes necessary to do so. Other thinkers say that necessity through a free choice does not conflict with freedom. God may freely create the world even if creation is necessary from then on and impossible in eternity. — س ره

A choice must be preceded by knowledge, will, intention, and power. In this account, God’s knowledge helps bring what He knows into being, and His will takes effect. The action would also depend on the chosen time being present. There is another problem: will is the final part of the complete cause, so the effect should follow it without delay. If a choice occurs at one time but the action only happens later, that choice is more like a general plan—such as deciding in winter to build in summer—than a specific will to act then. — س ره
These thinkers compare the will’s relation to the power to act with the relation between necessity and possibility. — س ره
That is, it is impossible for the event to happen before its appointed time. — س ره
The claim is that will follows knowledge and carries out what knowledge judges possible—that is, something that can happen later, not before. But this has already been rejected. — س ره

This differs from the earlier view that God wills what He knows will happen. That view makes His knowledge the cause of the event’s beginning. This view says instead that having a beginning belongs to the event itself. — س ره

Someone may object that allowing a choice without a reason denies a purpose that explains the action and blocks the proof of an agent that brings things about. The reply is that if an option can win without a reason, it also seems to be favored without a cause. The issue is which option becomes real, not merely whether the agent prefers it. Also, for those who accept a purpose as what makes an agent act, denying that purpose is like denying the agent itself. — س ره

Someone may say that the other thinkers do not claim God’s knowledge follows what happens; they only say He knows which things will and will not happen. But the Ashʿarites are known to say that knowledge follows what is known. If instead they say God’s knowledge is active and comes before the thing, they face the problems of treating it as eternal and compelled. There is also a direct argument: knowing a thing as it is requires that it exist. We cannot know a nonexistent thing as it is. If it had no existence or nature for the knower, how could it be known and distinguished? This argument also assumes from the start the very timing it needs to explain. — س ره

This means God’s eternal knowledge of a thing as it is. If that knowledge depends on the thing’s existing, the explanation goes in a circle. If it depends on the thing’s essence, it treats nonexistent essences as real. Another account says that essences are fixed through their dependence on God’s existence, but the thinkers under discussion have not reached that view, much less the idea that all things exist within the simple reality of God in a higher and more unified way. In any case, God’s eternal knowledge is active; it does not single out one particular time for a thing to begin. — س ره
This alludes to a reply to the view that time itself determines when an event begins. — س ره

The argument proves that God’s creative activity and causing continue without end; it does not prove that the things He creates are eternal. This is what the author means below by “the universal act” and “creation in general.” He began from the view of the most accomplished philosophers. But saying that everything besides God and His attributes is eternal would be disbelief and error, according to the thinkers of Maʿārij al-Kamāl, among the leading philosophers. This is how the argument should be stated, though the point is difficult to grasp. — ن ره

The argument does apply to events that continually renew themselves: the world of nature is always changing and cannot be eternal in the sense of remaining fixed. Its place at the receiving end of God’s giving is part of its nature, yet God’s giving does not cease. — س ره
There is a difference between the possibility of existing without a beginning and the possibility itself having no beginning. — س ره
This is remarkable: what explains why events begin also explains why God’s activity continues. — س ره
That is, what connects events to the Eternal is one continuous reality, not something preceded by a definite or imagined time. — س ره

This objection likely comes from misunderstanding Avicenna. He means a complete cause. An effect cannot be causally prior to its complete cause, and something that accompanies a cause cannot be earlier than its effect in time, since cause and effect exist at the same time. Priority by nature is not relevant here either. Priority, posteriority, and being together by nature concern incomplete causes; an incomplete cause cannot be considered alongside a complete cause, whether inside or outside it. So Avicenna is right that there is no priority in this case. — ط مد

For example, the outer sphere that exists with the second intellect is ahead of the inner sphere in rank and honor. But the priority by nature mentioned by the objector is the role of the last part of a complete cause, often called “the cause,” and of the removal of an obstacle. Both exist together with the complete cause. — س ره

This kind of priority does not follow just because two things happen together. Sunrise may coincide with a hand moving, and that hand movement may come before a key moves; the sun does not therefore come before the key. By contrast, the outer sphere and the second intellect exist together in their own order because both are effects of one cause. — س ره

Someone may ask how a feature can exist together with the thing that has it. The answer is that this is a matter of rank within the order of kinds. We can choose a broader kind, such as substance, or a specific kind, such as human being, as our starting point. Being together in one sense does not rule out priority or posteriority in another. — س ره

Al-Rāzī argues that if what accompanies something prior can be prior in one case, it should also be prior in the other. But this compares two different claims: whether one effect can have two causes, and whether one cause can have two effects. — س ره

Al-Rāzī may have a point. His objection concerns priority by nature, not only priority through causation. Something accompanying what is prior by nature may itself be prior by nature when the two are essentially linked, as animal and rationality are in relation to a human being. Or they may merely happen to be together, as sunrise, or Zayd’s arrival, may coincide with a hand movement that comes before a key moves. Perhaps the difference lies in what “together” means. — س ره

Causality is a feature a thing can have only once it exists. But in this proposed circle, the thing’s existence would come from something else. So it would first be an effect of that other thing and only then a cause of it. This is how the circular argument should be set out. — ن ره
That is, even though the impossibility of the conclusion is already plain, another argument is offered for it. — س ره

A difference that exists only in how we think of things is not enough to make opposites coexist. Priority and posteriority, and cause and effect, are unlike the knower and the known: the latter can be related in both directions, while the former cannot. Nor is the author’s denial here self-evident, so questioning it does not violate the rules of debate. — س ره

Since the argument is stated without qualification, it seems to claim that possibility and necessity conflict both in meaning and in reality. The author denies that they conflict in reality. Had the argument been offered only as a pointer to the proof, this loose wording would have been common enough. — س ره
